title: Galileo, honestly (1633)
hook: the Church condemned Galileo; in 1992 John Paul II acknowledged the error

segments.voice: Yesterday, Edmund Campion, Margaret Clitherow, and the hidden places in their houses, the priest holes. Your line was hidden priests. Today, a story the Church tells against itself.

A tube of glass and wood, pointed at the night sky over Italy. Through it, the moon has mountains. Jupiter has small lights circling it. The man at the eyepiece writes it all up in a short book with a Latin title, the Starry Messenger. He is a Catholic, a professor, and very sure of himself. What he's seeing points to an idea that the earth moves around the sun, and some in the Church will call that idea against the Scriptures. His name is Galileo.
screen: `MOUNTAINS ON THE MOON.` → `THE STARRY MESSENGER.` → `THE EARTH MOVES.`

segments.voice: First, the argument. Galileo's critics pointed to passages like the one where Joshua commands the sun to stand still. If the sun stands still, they said, it must normally move. Galileo answered in a long letter, quoting a churchman of his day: the Holy Spirit means to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go. Scripture, he argued, speaks the way ordinary people speak about sunrise. Second, the condemnation. The Holy Office in Rome ruled against the idea, and later put Galileo on trial. He was made to kneel and formally renounce the view that the earth moves. He spent the rest of his life confined to his house near Florence, and kept working. He was not burned, and he remained a Catholic. Third, the legend. People say that as he rose from his knees he muttered, and yet it moves. It's a good line, but it isn't in the trial records; it's a story told later. Fourth, the admission. Centuries later, Pope John Paul the Second asked for the case to be studied again. Speaking to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, he acknowledged that the theologians who condemned Galileo had erred, and called the affair a tragic mutual misunderstanding. A pope had said, in public, that the condemnation was a mistake. Some Catholics pair this with the Psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God." For those who pray it, the Psalm and the telescope look at the same sky.
screen: `THE SUN STANDS STILL?` · `HOW TO GO TO HEAVEN, NOT HOW IT GOES.` · `CONDEMNED, CONFINED, STILL CATHOLIC.` · `AND YET IT MOVES: A LATER STORY.` · then, large: `THE ERROR, ADMITTED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you got wrong and haven't quite owned: a judgment about someone, an argument you shouldn't have won, something you insisted on that turned out false. Let it be what it was, then picture saying it plainly to the person it touched: I was wrong about that. If you pray, bring it to God first; if you don't, simply practice the words.
Galileo. The Catholic astronomer whose telescope findings backed a moving earth, who was condemned in Rome, and whose case a pope later called an error.
Your line: the error, admitted. It took centuries, and it still counted. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Vatican keeps an observatory and a Pontifical Academy of Sciences, and Catholic teaching holds that faith and reason cannot truly contradict each other.

chat.says: Wasn't Galileo burned at the stake by the Church for saying the earth moves?
options: No. He was tried and confined to his house, stayed Catholic, and a pope later called it an error.
Yes. He was burned in Rome after refusing to take back his view that the earth moves.
No. The Church agreed with him then; the trial was only about his rude letters.
chat.meaning: Galileo was made to renounce the moving earth and confined to his house, not burned; John Paul the Second acknowledged the theologians had erred.

Starry Messenger.meaning: Galileo's short book of telescope findings

Holy Office.meaning: the Roman office that judged questions of doctrine

Pontifical Academy of Sciences.meaning: the papal academy where John Paul spoke about Galileo

Florence.meaning: the Italian city near Galileo's house

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's year for John Paul II's address is not said in the voice ('centuries later'); the title keeps 1633.
Telescope findings in the Starry Messenger (mountains on the moon, moons of Jupiter): confirm the hook's phrasing.
Letter to Christina: the saying about heaven is attributed by Galileo to an ecclesiastic of the time (traditionally Cardinal Baronius); paraphrased. Confirm.
Abjuration while kneeling, house arrest at Arcetri, 'not burned', 'remained a Catholic': standard account; confirm.
'Eppur si muove' described as a later story not in the trial records; confirm.

John Paul II's address paraphrased: theologians' error, 'tragic mutual incomprehension' (rendered 'tragic mutual misunderstanding'). Confirm wording and whether the address should be called an acknowledgment of error.
